passage: The first month after we moved to Nashik, I cried in the bathroom most nights so nobody would hear. I'm Vaibhav, and I thought I was the only person in the world who felt so lost. One night Papa knocked and sat on the edge of the tub. He told me that when he was nine, his family moved from a village to Pune, and he hid under the stairs at his new school for a whole week. 'I thought everyone could tell I didn't belong,' he said. I stared at him. Papa, who talks to everyone? After that, every Sunday he took me and my little sister Hafsa to the Godavari ghats for vada pav. It became our thing. Slowly, Nashik started to feel like somewhere I lived, not just somewhere I was.

qa.q: Where did Papa hide at his new school?
qa.a: Under the stairs, for a whole week.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel on hearing Papa's story?
qa.a: Surprised and much less alone; Vaibhav had thought nobody else ever felt so lost 🙂

qa.q: What small routine helped settle Vaibhav?
qa.a: Sunday trips to the Godavari ghats for vada pav with Papa and Hafsa.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt seeing Vaibhav so lost?
qa.a: Worried and protective, and reminded of his own lonely week, which is why he chose to share it.

grounding: A child who feels lost after a move hears that the father once felt the same, feels less alone, and settles through a weekly outing.

passage:
Counsellor's note, by Bhavna Kulkarni, school counselling room.
Ramesh, Class 4, new this term, came in with his father after two weeks of eating lunch alone and saying little. Ramesh sat with his arms folded. His father spoke first. 'When we moved to Delhi, I was younger than you. I didn't speak Hindi well. I felt lost for a whole year.' Ramesh looked up for the first time. 'A whole year?' 'Nearly. It got better when my mother started taking me to the Sunday market.' Ramesh's arms uncrossed. He admitted that he misses his old cricket ground most. We agreed on a small plan: a Saturday outing with his father to find a new ground. I will check in with Ramesh next Friday.

qa.q: What does Ramesh miss most?
qa.a: His old cricket ground.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's arms uncrossing suggest?
qa.a: He felt less alone and more open after hearing that his father had also felt lost.

qa.q: What plan did they agree on?
qa.a: A Saturday outing with his father to find a new cricket ground, with a check-in next Friday.

qa.q: How might the father feel sharing his own lost year?
qa.a: A little exposed but hopeful, wanting Ramesh to know the feeling can pass.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a new boy opening up after his father shares that he too felt lost in a new place.

passage: When Dadaji went into hospital with his heart, everyone at home spoke in low voices and stopped talking when I came in. My name is Pranav, and that silence frightened me more than anything. I lay awake thinking, what if he dies and nobody tells me? On the third day I asked Ramesh Chacha straight out, 'Is Dadaji going to die?' He didn't laugh or change the subject. He said, 'His heart is weak, and the doctors are working hard. We don't know yet. I'll tell you when we know more.' It was scary, but less scary than the silence. That evening Chacha took me to the hospital. I held Dadaji's hand and showed him my drawing of our mango tree. He squeezed my fingers.

qa.q: What did Pranav show Dadaji?
qa.a: A drawing of their mango tree.

qa.q: Why did the silence at home frighten Pranav?
qa.a: Pranav felt afraid and shut out, lying awake worried that Dadaji might die without anyone saying so.

qa.q: What helped Pranav's fear?
qa.a: Asking Ramesh Chacha an honest question, getting a truthful answer, then visiting Dadaji to hold his hand and share a drawing.

qa.q: What might Dadaji have felt when Pranav held his hand?
qa.a: Comforted and loved; he squeezed Pranav's fingers.

grounding: A child afraid a grandfather may die asks an adult an honest question, gets a truthful answer, and sits with him.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, by Nazia Siddiqui.
Vishal was quiet all morning and drew the same picture three times: a bed with a small figure in it. At break I sat with him. 'My Nanaji is in hospital,' he whispered. 'Nobody tells me anything. Is he going to die?' His lip was trembling. I told him I did not know, that it was a good question, and that the people who could answer it were his parents. With his permission I phoned his mother at lunch. She came at home time and knelt beside him. 'Nanaji is very ill, and the doctors are helping him. You can visit on Sunday and take your drawing.' Vishal held her hand tightly and asked two more questions. She answered both.

qa.q: What did Vishal draw three times?
qa.a: A bed with a small figure in it.

qa.q: What did Vishal's trembling lip show?
qa.a: He was frightened that Nanaji might die and upset that nobody was telling him anything.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped?
qa.a: Sat with Vishal, admitted not knowing, and phoned his mother that day so she could give him simple, honest answers.

qa.q: How might his mother have felt learning Vishal was so worried?
qa.a: Probably sorry she hadn't explained sooner and eager to comfort him, since she came, knelt and answered his questions.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy frightened about his grandfather's illness, and adults giving him honest answers the same day.

passage:
Saturday
Dear Diary,
It's Elizabeth again. Granny is still in bed since her fall, and the house smells of balm. Mum said Granny must rest and I mustn't tire her. I didn't know what to do, so I took my library book and sat on the stool beside her bed. I read her two chapters about the girl with the runaway pony. I did all the voices. Granny kept her eyes closed, but she smiled at the funny bits, and once she laughed so much she coughed. When I stopped, she said, 'Same time tomorrow, Lizzie?' I felt so warm. I can't make her leg better. But I can do this. Varun wants to come tomorrow and do the pony noises.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth's library book about?
qa.a: A girl with a runaway pony.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when Granny asked for the same time tomorrow?
qa.a: Warm and happy, glad that simply sitting and reading was helping Granny 🤍

qa.q: What does Elizabeth understand about helping Granny?
qa.a: That Elizabeth can't make Granny's leg better, but being there and reading is still a real help.

qa.q: What was the reading like for Granny?
qa.a: Restful and cheering; she smiled at the funny bits, laughed, and wanted it again tomorrow.

grounding: A child sits and reads to a resting grandmother, learning that being present is enough.

passage: The fan had stopped with the power cut, and Paati lay on the cot in the front room of their house near Thanjavur, eyes closed, forehead damp. Bhavna didn't know how to make her better. Keerthana, her cousin, whispered, 'Leave her. Grown-ups will handle it.' But Bhavna picked up the palm-leaf fan and sat on the floor beside the cot. She waved it slowly. Then she unfolded the morning newspaper and read out the headlines, stumbling over long words. Paati's lips twitched. 'Read me the rice prices, kanna.' Bhavna read them. She read the temple festival dates too. When Amma came in, Paati was asleep, and Bhavna was still fanning, her arm aching, feeling strangely calm.

qa.q: What did Bhavna use to fan Paati?
qa.a: The palm-leaf fan.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna feel strangely calm by the end?
qa.a: Though she couldn't cure Paati, staying close and helping made her feel useful and loving instead of helpless.

qa.q: What did Bhavna understand that Keerthana did not?
qa.a: That a child can help just by being there, fanning and reading, without needing to fix the illness.

qa.q: What might Paati have felt as Bhavna read the headlines?
qa.a: Comforted and amused; her lips twitched and she asked for the rice prices before falling asleep.

grounding: A village girl sits with her ill grandmother, fanning her and reading aloud, and finds that being present is enough.

passage: In the hospital corridor, Ammi and Abbu stood by the window, whispering. Every time Parveen came near, they stopped. 'Go and sit, beta. It's nothing.' But it wasn't nothing. Nanajaan had been wheeled through the swinging doors an hour ago. Parveen sat on the plastic chair and bit her nails until one bled. Sister Reena, the nurse at the desk, handed her a tissue and then spoke quietly to Ammi. Ammi came over and sat down. 'You want to know what's happening?' Parveen nodded hard. 'Nanajaan's lungs are sick. The doctors are giving him medicine and oxygen. He's tired, but he can see you for five minutes.' Parveen's shoulders dropped. She went in and held his hand, and he winked at her.

qa.q: What did Sister Reena hand Parveen?
qa.a: A tissue.

qa.q: What did Parveen's nail-biting show?
qa.a: She was scared and anxious, because the whispering made her fear the worst about Nanajaan.

qa.q: What changed things for Parveen?
qa.a: Ammi sat down, gave simple, honest information and let her visit Nanajaan for five minutes.

qa.q: Why might Ammi and Abbu have whispered at first?
qa.a: They wanted to protect Parveen from worry, not realising the secrecy made her more frightened.

grounding: In a hospital corridor a girl grows more scared while her parents whisper, and calms once her mother explains honestly and lets her visit.

passage:
Monday. Pema noticed her grandfather's room was empty and the phone kept ringing. Her father, Anand, said Popo had 'gone away for a few days'. His voice sounded wrong. That night Pema couldn't sleep, imagining terrible things.
Wednesday. Pema heard her parents whispering the word 'hospital' in the kitchen. She burst in. 'Tell me! I'm not a baby!' Her mother's face crumpled.
Friday. Both parents sat with her on the sofa. 'Popo has an infection in his chest. He's in hospital so the doctors can help him breathe better. We should have told you sooner.' Pema cried, but it was a cleaner kind of crying. On Saturday she visited Popo with a flask of butter tea and helped him sip it.

qa.q: What did Pema take on her visit?
qa.a: A flask of butter tea.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling on Monday night?
qa.a: Scared and uneasy; she could not sleep, imagining terrible things because her father's voice sounded wrong.

qa.q: What did the parents do right on Friday?
qa.a: They sat with Pema, explained simply and honestly, admitted they should have told her sooner, and then let her visit.

qa.q: What was it like for Pema's mother when Pema burst in?
qa.a: Painful; her face crumpled, perhaps as she realised the secret was hurting Pema.

grounding: Over a week a girl grows more frightened while her parents hide her grandfather's illness, until they explain honestly and let her help.

passage: The day before Aaji went to hospital, she asked me to thread her needle, and I snapped, 'Can't you see I'm busy?' I was watching cartoons. I'm Madhuri, and I've never felt as bad as I did the next morning, when Papa said Aaji had had a stroke. For two days I couldn't eat properly. My brother Ujjwal found me crying behind the water tank. 'You're not a bad person,' he said. 'You're sad because you love her.' On Sunday we visited. Aaji's mouth was a little crooked, but her eyes knew me. I held her hand and said, 'Sorry I was rude about the needle. I love you, Aaji.' She squeezed back. I still feel a little bad, but it's lighter now.

qa.q: What did Aaji ask Madhuri to do?
qa.a: To thread her needle.

qa.q: Why couldn't Madhuri eat properly for two days?
qa.a: Madhuri felt guilty and scared after being rude to Aaji just before she fell ill.

qa.q: What helped Madhuri with the guilt?
qa.a: Ujjwal's kind words, then visiting Aaji and saying sorry and I love you to her face.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see Madhuri's tears?
qa.a: As a sign of love, not badness; he says the sadness comes from loving Aaji.

grounding: A child feels guilty for being rude to a grandmother before she fell ill, then says sorry and I love you.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday, by Samir Khan.
Ishita (Class 5) came in during break, eyes red. Two weeks ago her grandmother moved in with the family after an illness. Ishita told me that on the first day she refused to hug her because 'the room smelled of medicine', and said, 'I wish you'd gone to Masi's house instead.' Now her grandmother is back in hospital. 'What if she thinks I hate her?' Ishita sobbed. I told her that feeling guilty shows how much she cares, and that it does not have to stay forever. Together we made a card. She wrote: 'Dadi, I'm sorry for what I said. I love you. Please get well.' I phoned her father, who agreed to take her to the hospital that evening.

qa.q: What did Ishita say the room smelled of?
qa.a: Medicine.

qa.q: What was Ishita worried about?
qa.a: She felt guilty and frightened that Dadi might think she hated her after her unkind words.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take?
qa.a: Explained that guilt shows care and need not last forever, helped Ishita make a card, and phoned her father so she could visit that evening.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel reading Ishita's card?
qa.a: Touched and comforted; the apology and 'I love you' would show her Ishita's real feelings.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a girl guilty about unkind words to her ill grandmother, helped to apologise and visit.

passage: 'Asif, come and sit on the step with your old Bhupen Dadu. I heard about your Nana. I'm so sorry. You look angry, and that's all right. When I was ten, my own grandfather died in the monsoon. I felt nothing at first, just empty, like a bucket with a hole in it. Then I was furious at everyone who kept eating and talking. I kicked the gate so hard my toe went blue. My mother didn't scold me. She let me ask her every question, even silly ones, like whether he could still hear the rain. At the shraddha, she let me place his favourite betel leaf. The sadness came back for years, in waves, at odd times. It still visits sometimes. But it's softer now, like he was.'

qa.q: What did young Bhupen place at the shraddha?
qa.a: His grandfather's favourite betel leaf.

qa.q: What did young Bhupen feel in the days after his grandfather died?
qa.a: First empty, then furious at everyone carrying on as normal; both were part of his grief.

qa.q: What choice by his mother helped young Bhupen in the story?
qa.a: She didn't scold him for his anger, answered every question, and let him take part in the shraddha.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's mother have felt when he kicked the gate?
qa.a: Probably sad and worried for him, yet patient, choosing understanding over scolding.

grounding: An elder recalls the emptiness and anger of grief when his grandfather died, and how questions and rituals helped.

passage: The call came at midnight, and by dawn Uday was squeezed into a crowded general coach with Papa, heading to Ajja's village for the funeral. There was no seat. Uday stood by the door, numb. Ajja had taught him to swim in the river only last summer. How could he just stop? Near Hubli, Uday suddenly snapped at a man who bumped him, then burst into tears. Papa pulled him close. 'Ask me anything,' Papa said. Uday asked where Ajja was now, and whether dying hurt. Papa answered what he could and said 'I don't know' to the rest. At the village, his cousin Samir took him to the river. They sat on the rock where Ajja used to dry his towel and told Ajja stories until the conch sounded for the rites.

qa.q: Where did Uday stand on the train?
qa.a: By the door of the crowded general coach.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he snapped at the man?
qa.a: After feeling numb, his grief came out as anger and confusion, and then broke into tears.

qa.q: What helped Uday on the journey and at the village?
qa.a: Papa holding him and answering his questions honestly, and sharing Ajja stories with Samir before the rites.

qa.q: What might it be like for Papa on that train?
qa.a: Hard, since he was likely grieving too while comforting Uday and admitting what he didn't know.

grounding: On a crowded overnight journey to a funeral, a boy's grief shows as numbness and anger, and questions and shared memories help.

passage:
Tuesday night
Diary, it's Gargi. Tonight I found Maa crying in the kitchen with the tap running so nobody would hear. Dadu, her baba, is very sick in a Kolkata hospital, and she can't go till Friday. I stood in the doorway and felt useless. I wanted to say something clever that would fix it, but nothing came. So I just went and hugged her from behind, around her waist. She put her wet hand on mine, and we stood like that while the tap ran. Then Madhav toddled in wanting milk, and Maa laughed a bit and wiped her face. I didn't fix anything. But she held my hand for a long time. I didn't know grown-ups cried like that. It's okay, I think.

qa.q: Why was the tap running?
qa.a: So nobody would hear Maa crying.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel standing in the doorway?
qa.a: Useless and helpless, wishing for something clever to say that would fix it.

qa.q: What did Gargi do that helped, even without words?
qa.a: Gargi hugged Maa from behind and stayed close, without trying to fix her feelings.

qa.q: What might Maa have felt when Gargi hugged her?
qa.a: Comforted and less alone; she put her hand on Gargi's and held it for a long time.

grounding: A child finds a mother crying about her own father's illness, feels helpless, and simply hugs and stays near.

passage: At dusk, in their village near Bathinda, Amandeep found his mother, Rekha, sitting on the charpai by the cattle shed, the phone still in her lap. Her shoulders were shaking. Nanaji was in hospital in Patiala, and the news was not good. Amandeep froze. He had never seen Mummy cry like this. His stomach churned. He wanted to run to the fields and not come back till everything was fixed. Instead he sat beside her on the charpai. He didn't say anything. He just leaned his head on her arm. After a while she wrapped her arm around him. 'Your Nanaji taught me to milk that buffalo,' she said, pointing. They watched the buffalo chew in the fading light together.

qa.q: Where was Nanaji in hospital?
qa.a: In Patiala.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's churning stomach show?
qa.a: He felt scared and helpless, seeing Mummy cry like that for the first time.

qa.q: What did Amandeep choose instead of running away?
qa.a: To sit beside her quietly and lean on her arm, staying near without trying to fix anything.

qa.q: How did the moment change for Rekha?
qa.a: She seemed comforted enough to wrap her arm around him and share a memory of her father.

grounding: A village boy finds his mother crying over her father's illness and stays close without trying to fix it.

passage: 'Pooja, you say Meenu hardly spoke all day because her grandmother is in hospital? Come, your Zeenat Khala will tell you what I learned at your age. My friend Farida went silent for a whole week once. Her grandmother, who lived with them, was very ill. Everyone kept saying, "Don't worry, she'll be fine!" and Farida just shrank smaller. I didn't know what to say, so I said nothing. I sat next to her under the jamun tree at recess and shared my aloo paratha, half and half, every day. On Friday she suddenly started talking about her grandmother's songs. I only listened. Years later Farida told me that in that week, I was the only one who didn't make her pretend.'

qa.q: What did young Zeenat share at recess?
qa.a: Her aloo paratha, half and half.

qa.q: How did young Zeenat feel about not knowing what to say?
qa.a: Unsure and awkward, but she chose to stay close quietly rather than say something empty.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Farida most?
qa.a: Sitting with her and sharing food without pushing questions or saying it would be fine, then just listening.

qa.q: How did 'Don't worry, she'll be fine!' feel to Farida?
qa.a: It made her shrink smaller; she felt she had to pretend instead of being allowed to be sad.

grounding: An aunt recalls sitting quietly with a friend whose grandmother was ill, being a kind presence rather than offering empty reassurance.

passage: It was sports day, and the sun blazed over the ground. Loudspeakers crackled, and the whole class cheered for the relay. Only Ankita sat on the steps, knees pulled up. That morning she had told Sonali in one sentence, 'Nani's in the ICU.' Then nothing more. Sonali's team needed her for the sack race in ten minutes. She looked at the queue, then at Ankita. She told her captain she'd be back in time and sat down beside Ankita with her packet of peanut chikki. She broke it in half and held one piece out. Ankita took it. Sonali didn't ask questions or say it would be fine. They just watched the relay together. When the whistle blew for the sack race, Ankita whispered, 'Go. Thanks for sitting.'

qa.q: What did Sonali share with Ankita?
qa.a: Her packet of peanut chikki, broken in half.

qa.q: Why did Sonali sit down beside Ankita despite the race?
qa.a: She felt concerned and caring for Ankita, whose Nani was in the ICU, and didn't want her to sit alone.

qa.q: What made Sonali's support gentle?
qa.a: She shared food and stayed close without pressing with questions or promising things would be fine.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt with Sonali beside her?
qa.a: Less alone and grateful; she took the chikki and thanked Sonali for sitting.

grounding: On a busy sports day a girl sits quietly with a friend whose grandmother is very ill, sharing a snack and not pushing.

passage: In the hospital café in Berlin, Jana stirred her hot chocolate and watched doctors in green hurry past. Opa was upstairs having an operation on his heart. 'What are they actually doing to him?' she asked. Her mother, Ines, drew on a napkin: a heart with little doors. 'One door isn't closing properly. They're putting in a new one, so the blood flows the right way.' Jana studied the drawing. It made the people in green seem less scary. 'Will it work?' Ines was honest. 'The doctors do this often, and they're good at it. But we won't know for sure until he wakes up.' Jana folded the napkin into her pocket. She was still nervous, but now she could picture what was happening, and that helped.

qa.q: What did Ines draw on the napkin?
qa.a: A heart with little doors.

qa.q: How did the drawing change how Jana felt?
qa.a: It made the doctors seem less scary; she was still nervous but calmer because she could picture what was happening.

qa.q: What helped Jana trust the doctors?
qa.a: Asking her mother a direct question and getting a simple, honest explanation, including that nobody could be sure yet.

qa.q: What might Ines have been feeling while she answered Jana?
qa.a: Probably worried about Opa herself, yet careful to stay calm and honest for Jana.

grounding: While her grandfather has an operation, a girl asks her mother what the doctors are doing and trusts them more once she understands.

passage: The hospital ward hummed and beeped. Kashish stood at the foot of Nanu's bed, staring at the tubes running from his arm to a big humming machine. Her hands were cold. 'Mummy, is the machine hurting him?' she whispered. Her mother, Jahnavi, squeezed her shoulder. 'Let's ask.' When the doctor came round, Mummy said, 'Doctor, can you explain it simply for Kashish?' The doctor crouched down. 'Nanu's kidneys are tired. This machine cleans his blood for them. It doesn't hurt, but it makes him sleepy.' Kashish nodded slowly. 'Will he get better?' 'We're working on it. Some days will be good, some not so good.' Kashish breathed out. She pulled a chair close and held Nanu's free hand.

qa.q: What does the machine do, according to the doctor?
qa.a: It cleans Nanu's blood for his tired kidneys.

qa.q: What did Kashish's cold hands suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was frightened by the tubes and the machine and worried it was hurting Nanu.

qa.q: What helped Kashish cope in the ward?
qa.a: Asking Mummy, who got the doctor to explain simply, and then sitting close and holding Nanu's hand.

qa.q: How might Nanu feel with Kashish holding his hand?
qa.a: Comforted and less alone during a tiring treatment.

grounding: In a hospital ward a girl trusts the doctors more once a simple explanation is asked for, and prepares for good and bad days.

passage: The week Dida was in hospital, my sister Sabina and I fought about everything. The remote. The last biscuit. Whose turn it was to feed the fish. I'm Anirban, and I remember shouting, 'You always ruin everything!' over a pencil. Sabina threw it at me and ran to her room. Then I heard her crying through the door, and it wasn't about the pencil. I sat outside her door. It was really about Dida, for both of us. We were scared, and it came out as anger. I knocked. 'Sorry about the pencil. And the biscuit.' She opened the door a crack. 'I'm scared about Dida,' she said. 'Me too.' We sat on her bed and made a get-well card together, taking turns with the same pencil.

qa.q: What did Anirban shout over the pencil?
qa.a: 'You always ruin everything!'

qa.q: What feeling was really behind the fights, according to Anirban?
qa.a: Both of them were scared about Dida, and the fear came out as anger and irritation.

qa.q: What turned the fight around?
qa.a: Anirban knocked and apologised, and they named their fear and comforted each other by making a card together.

qa.q: How was Sabina feeling when she threw the pencil?
qa.a: Scared about Dida and overwhelmed, so the pencil fight was really about her worry.

grounding: Two siblings snap at each other while their grandmother is in hospital, then see it is fear, apologise and comfort each other.

passage:
Note for Didi and Jiju, from Ganga Mausi, Saturday night.
The children are fine, but I want you to know about today. Chinmay and Pari fought three times before lunch, over the swing, the TV and a hair clip. When Pari said, 'Nana might die and you don't even care,' Chinmay yelled back and slammed the door. I didn't scold. I sat them both at the dining table and asked, 'Are you two angry, or scared?' Pari started crying first, then Chinmay. We talked about Nana for a long time. Afterwards Chinmay said sorry to Pari on his own, and she gave him the hair clip to fix his fringe. They slept in the same room tonight. Please call them tomorrow morning.

qa.q: How many times did Chinmay and Pari fight before lunch?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when he yelled and slammed the door?
qa.a: Scared about Nana and hurt by Pari's words, so the fear came out as anger.

qa.q: What did Ganga Mausi do that helped?
qa.a: She didn't scold; she sat them down and asked whether they were angry or scared, so they could talk about Nana.

qa.q: How might Pari have felt when Chinmay said sorry?
qa.a: Relieved and closer to him; she gave him the hair clip for his fringe.

grounding: An aunt's note describes two siblings snapping at each other out of fear for their grandfather, and helping them name it and make up.
